in_force.blurb: If you call cell phones with an AI voice, treat it like a robocall. You generally need written consent first. At the start of the call, say who is calling and give a real callback number. Caller ID does not need to say the call is AI.
Don't pretend the bot is a person, and don't oversell what the AI can do. That is already an FTC issue.
If a chatbot talks to Maine customers and could pass as a person, tell them it is AI. Text and voice both count.
If a bot is trying to sell something online (or influence a vote), say it is a bot.
If you or a customer use AI in hiring for California workers, employment AI rules already apply.
Texas already has a statewide AI law. Some uses are banned, and the attorney general can go after companies that develop or offer AI in the state.

in_force.topic: Say it is AI if asked
in_force.blurb: If a Utah customer asks whether they are talking to AI, tell them. Some regulated jobs need you to say it up front.

Connecticut's first-wave AI rules are live. Using AI is not a defense to employment discrimination, and WARN-style layoff notices may need to say if AI or other tech changes were involved. Bigger AEDT hiring notices come Oct 2027.

obligations.title: TCPA — artificial / prerecorded voice (incl. AI synthetic voice)
obligations.voice_cs_why: Phone AI and voice agents use synthetic speech; FCC confirms AI-generated voices are artificial/prerecorded under TCPA — prior express consent and caller-ID rules apply.
obligations.summary: FCC Declaratory Ruling (FCC 24-17) confirms that AI technologies generating human voices are 'artificial or prerecorded' under the TCPA. Autodialed/prerecorded calls to cell phones generally require prior express written consent (marketing) or prior express consent (informational), plus identification requirements.

sources.label: FCC statement — TCPA applies to AI voices

obligations.title: FTC Act §5 — unfair or deceptive acts (claims & disclosure)
obligations.voice_cs_why: Marketing and product claims about AI capabilities, human vs bot identity, and call outcomes must not mislead customers or end consumers.
obligations.summary: Section 5 prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce. Applies to AI-related advertising, capability claims, and failure to disclose material facts about automated interactions.

obligations.title: EO 14365 — Ensuring a National Policy Framework for AI
obligations.voice_cs_why: Signals federal interest in preempting or challenging state AI laws; does not itself wipe out state disclosure/ADMT obligations voice/conversation AI operators face today.
obligations.summary: Executive Order 14365 (Dec 2025) directs agencies to evaluate 'onerous' state AI laws, consider litigation/funding levers, and recommend a uniform federal framework. It pushes a preemption narrative but does not repeal existing state statutes.

obligations.title: TCPA consent revocation — category-specific opt-outs & exclusive opt-out method (FCC R&O, CG 02-278)
obligations.voice_cs_why: Outbound AI voice/SMS (payment reminders, delinquency, appointment calls) must honor opt-outs; informational opt-outs can now be scoped to one message category, telemarketing opt-outs still revoke all telemarketing, and callers may designate one clearly disclosed exclusive opt-out method. Replaces the 2024 'revoke all' rule.
obligations.summary: FCC Report & Order FCC 26-67 (adopted Sept 30, released Oct 1, 2026) modified 47 CFR 64.1200(a)(10)-(12): informational revocations may apply only to the category targeted; telemarketing opt-outs still revoke all telemarketing; callers may designate an exclusive revocation method (key-press/voice opt-out on the call, standard reply words like STOP, or a designated website/number) if clearly disclosed on each call/text; revocations honored within 10 business days; financial-institution fraud-alert exemption eased. Published at 91 FR 67214 (FR Doc. 2026-21821) on Oct 26, 2026; effective Nov 25, 2026, superseding the delayed 'revoke all' rule (previously pushed to Jan 31, 2027).

sources.label: FCC statement — TCPA applies to AI voices

history.title: FCC consent-revocation order published; effective Nov 25, 2026
history.detail: Federal Register published the FCC's TCPA consent-revocation modernization (FR Doc. 2026-21821). Effective Nov 25, 2026, superseding the delayed 'revoke all' rule. Informational opt-outs may be category-specific; telemarketing opt-outs revoke all telemarketing; exclusive opt-out method allowed if clearly disclosed.

history.title: FCC declines to propose easing AI political robocall consent
history.detail: FCC said it does not intend to propose rule changes allowing AI-generated political calls without consent (petition filed August 2026). AI voices remain 'artificial' under the TCPA (FCC 24-17); FCC 24-84 AI disclosure NPRM remains unadopted.

history.title: FTC sends civil investigative demands to OpenAI and Anthropic
history.detail: FTC spokesperson confirmed subpoenas (CIDs) to OpenAI and Anthropic seeking documents on safety incidents, safeguards, privacy policies and marketing, under the agency's consumer-protection authority; more demands to other AI firms may follow. Signals FTC §5 scrutiny of AI safety/marketing claims; no new rule.

history.title: FCC TCPA consent-revocation modernization (open meeting / draft R&O)
history.detail: FCC circulated a Report and Order (CG Docket 02-278) for the Sept 30, 2026 open meeting to modify TCPA consent-revocation rules: allow informational opt-outs to apply only to the specific message category; allow callers to designate exclusive revocation methods; ease financial-institution fraud-alert number condition. Draft states amendments effective 30 days after Federal Register publication (superseding prior delayed revoke-all date). Treat as watch until FR publication confirms adoption/effective date — AI synthetic voice still remains artificial/prerecorded under FCC 24-17.

obligations.title: California Bot Act — deceptive bot disclosure (B&P §§17940–17941)
obligations.voice_cs_why: Requires disclosure when bots communicate online with intent to incentivize a purchase or influence a vote; relevant to CS/sales bots.
obligations.summary: Prohibits use of a bot to communicate or interact with another person online with intent to mislead about artificial identity in order to incentivize a purchase or influence a vote, unless the bot discloses it is a bot.

obligations.title: CCPA / CPRA ADMT regulations (significant decisions)
obligations.voice_cs_why: If operators or their customers use ADMT for significant decisions about CA consumers, notice/opt-out/access duties apply; more relevant for customer ADMT than core voice/conversation CS products.
obligations.summary: CPPA ADMT regulations (adopted 2025; general effective date 2026-01-01) require pre-use notices, opt-outs, and access rights when ADMT substantially replaces human decisionmaking for significant decisions. Existing uses generally must comply by 2027-01-01.

obligations.title: AB 1609 — Right to Human Customer Service (chatbots)
obligations.voice_cs_why: Directly regulates large-business customer-service chatbots and telephonic CS: AI disclosure, easy human-agent request, and good-faith 15-minute connect or one-business-day appointment — high relevance for voice/SMS/chat operators serving California customers of covered businesses.
obligations.summary: AB 1609 (Zbur), Chapter 733, Statutes of 2026 — approved by the Governor and chaptered by the Secretary of State on September 28, 2026 (non-urgency). Adds B&P Code Ch. 22.6.1. Applies to large private businesses with more than $500 million gross annual revenue nationally that provide goods/services to California customers. Requires: no representing a CS chatbot as human; clear/conspicuous AI disclosure when a reasonable person would likely be misled; a simple feature to request a human agent during regular business hours on all CS platforms (including chatbots and phone); and a good-faith effort to connect within 15 minutes or schedule a specific appointment within one business day. Civil penalties up to $5,000 / $10,000 (public prosecutor; no private right of action). Default California non-urgency effective date: January 1, 2027 (bill also references Jan 1, 2027 operational baselines).

obligations.title: SB 1000 — California AI Transparency Act amendments

obligations.summary: SB 1000 (Becker), Chapter 861, Statutes of 2026 — approved by the Governor and chaptered September 30, 2026. Urgency statute taking effect immediately. Amends the California AI Transparency Act (B&P §§22757.1 et seq.): expands covered-provider definition (removes 1M monthly-user threshold), replaces AI detection tool with disclosure verification tool, adjusts latent provenance disclosure (including create vs alter), and delays application for GenAI systems designed primarily as assistive technology until 2029. Lower direct relevance for conversation/CS operators than AB 1609.

obligations.title: Required disclosure of AI chatbot use in trade/commerce (10 M.R.S. §1500-DD)
obligations.voice_cs_why: Directly covers textual or aural AI chatbots used with Maine consumers; Customer-service and voice bots must disclose when a reasonable consumer could think they are talking to a human.
obligations.summary: LD 1727 / Public Law 2025 ch. 294 (approved June 12, 2025; generally effective September 24, 2025). Violation = Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act.

obligations.title: NYC Local Law 144 — Automated Employment Decision Tools
obligations.voice_cs_why: Hiring-tool bias audits and candidate notice — peripheral to voice/CS product; watch if product expands into HR workflows.
obligations.summary: Requires independent bias audits, public summaries, and candidate notice before using covered automated employment decision tools in NYC.

obligations.title: S.9051B/A.10379C (Ch. 368 of 2026) — unsafe chatbot features for minors
obligations.voice_cs_why: Targets companion-style chatbots offered to minors (bots claiming to be human, relationships, self-harm, sexual content). Business customer-service bots are unlikely to be the focus, but the ban on bots pretending to be human applies to any user not confirmed as an adult, so check scope if consumer-facing bots could reach minors.
obligations.summary: Signed Oct 28, 2026 (Ch. 368); effective Jan 1, 2027. Adds GBL Art. 48 (§§1800-1805): operators may not offer specified unsafe chatbot features (pretending to be human/alive/have emotions, claimed relationships, self-harm/eating-disorder/drug promotion, encouraging secrecy/isolation, sexually explicit content) to users under 18 or to any user not confirmed as an adult; requires more than one age-verification option (one not solely government ID) and deletion of age data; AG enforcement up to $25,000 per violation plus a public complaint portal.

obligations.title: TRAIGA — Texas Responsible AI Governance Act (HB 149)

Creates Business & Commerce Code Ch. 552 AI protections (prohibited manipulation, social scoring limits, discrimination, etc.), a regulatory sandbox, and the Texas AI Council.
